notes.definition: Higher tier: negative feedback is a control mechanism in which a change away from a normal level triggers a response that reverses the change, bringing the level back to normal. Thyroxine levels are controlled this way; adrenaline prepares the body for 'fight or flight'.
explanation: Negative feedback keeps conditions inside the body within a narrow range. When a level rises above normal, receptors detect the change and the response lowers the level. When it falls below normal, the response raises it. The level therefore stays close to the normal value, fluctuating slightly above and below it. You have already met examples: blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon, and (separate Biology) water control by ADH.

Thyroxine is a hormone produced by the thyroid gland in the neck. It stimulates the basal metabolic rate, which is the rate at which the body uses energy for chemical reactions while at rest. Thyroxine also plays an important role in growth and development, especially in children.

Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback. The pituitary gland releases TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone), which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. When the thyroxine level in the blood is high, it inhibits the release of TSH from the pituitary, so the thyroid releases less thyroxine. When the thyroxine level is low, TSH release is no longer inhibited, so more TSH is released and the thyroid releases more thyroxine.

Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys, in times of fear or stress. It increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles. This prepares the body for 'fight or flight'. More oxygen and glucose to the muscles means more respiration, releasing more energy for muscle contraction, so the body is ready to escape or confront a threat.

You need to interpret and explain simple diagrams of negative feedback control. Follow the loop: identify the normal level, what happens when it rises or falls, which gland responds, and how the hormone change brings the level back. The key idea is that the response always opposes the original change.
keyFacts: Higher only: this whole subtopic is Higher tier content.

keyTerms.definition: A control system in which a change from the normal level causes a response that returns the level to normal.
Hormone from the adrenal glands, released in fear or stress, that prepares the body for fight or flight.
Hormone from the thyroid gland that stimulates the basal metabolic rate and is important for growth and development.

workedExamples.title: Reading a negative feedback diagram
workedExamples.question: A diagram shows: pituitary → TSH → thyroid → thyroxine, with a dashed arrow from thyroxine back to the pituitary labelled 'inhibits'. Explain what happens if the thyroxine level rises above normal.
steps: High thyroxine inhibits the pituitary gland.
The thyroid is stimulated less, so it releases less thyroxine.
The thyroxine level falls back to normal: the response reversed the change.
workedExamples.answer: TSH release falls, so thyroxine release falls and the level returns to normal.

workedExamples.title: Percentage increase in heart rate
workedExamples.question: A person's heart rate rises from 72 to 126 beats per minute when adrenaline is released. Calculate the percentage increase.

workedExamples.title: Unit conversion: extra blood pumped
workedExamples.question: During fright, heart rate rises from 64 to 112 beats per minute. Each beat pumps 70 cm³ of blood. Calculate the increase in blood pumped per minute in dm³.
steps: Increase in rate = 112 − 64 = 48 beats per minute
workedExamples.answer: 3.36 dm³ more blood per minute, delivering more oxygen and glucose to muscles.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'negative feedback' means the level always goes down.
misconceptions.right: In fact negative feedback reverses any change: it lowers a level that is too high and raises one that is too low.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think adrenaline is made by the brain or the kidneys.
misconceptions.right: In fact adrenaline is made by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think thyroxine controls heart rate in fight or flight.
misconceptions.right: In fact thyroxine controls the basal metabolic rate over the long term; adrenaline gives the fast fight or flight response.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think high thyroxine stops the thyroid directly.
misconceptions.right: In fact high thyroxine inhibits the release of TSH from the pituitary gland, and less TSH means the thyroid makes less thyroxine.

realWorld: People with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) may feel tired, cold and gain weight; they can take thyroxine tablets.
Newborn babies in the UK are screened for low thyroxine because it is essential for normal growth and brain development.
Adrenaline injections (auto-injector pens) are used to treat severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis).
higherTier: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases heart rate and boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for fight or flight.
Thyroxine from the thyroid gland stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development.
Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback.
Explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline in the body, and interpret and explain simple diagrams of negative feedback control.
examTips: Define negative feedback by its effect: 'a change triggers a response that reverses the change'. Do not just say 'it keeps things constant'.
Quote the specification for adrenaline: increases heart rate and boosts delivery of oxygen AND glucose to the brain AND muscles.
In feedback diagrams, follow arrows one step at a time and use the words 'stimulates' and 'inhibits'.
Link thyroxine to 'basal metabolic rate'. Writing just 'metabolism' may not be credited.
If asked why muscles need more glucose and oxygen, mention respiration releasing energy for contraction.
summary: Negative feedback reverses changes to keep levels near normal.
Adrenaline (adrenal glands) is released in fear or stress for fight or flight.
Adrenaline raises heart rate and boosts oxygen and glucose to brain and muscles.
Thyroxine (thyroid gland) stimulates basal metabolic rate and growth and development.
TSH from the pituitary stimulates thyroxine release; high thyroxine inhibits TSH.
Interpret feedback diagrams by following each stimulate or inhibit step.

markScheme: 1 mark: Gland C (adrenal gland)
questions.explanation: Gland C is an adrenal gland, found on top of each kidney; it produces adrenaline. Gland A is the pituitary gland, gland B is the thyroid gland and gland D is the pancreas.

questions.question: Which gland produces thyroxine?
markScheme: 1 mark: Thyroid gland
questions.explanation: Thyroxine is made by the thyroid gland in the neck. The pituitary makes TSH, which controls the thyroid.

questions.question: When is adrenaline released into the blood?
options: When the blood is too dilute
In times of fear or stress
markScheme: 1 mark: In times of fear or stress
questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight when a person is frightened or stressed.

questions.question: Which process in the body does thyroxine stimulate?
options: The heart rate during fight or flight
markScheme: 1 mark: The basal metabolic rate
questions.explanation: Thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate. The fast rise in heart rate in fight or flight is caused by adrenaline; egg maturation by FSH; water reabsorption by ADH.

questions.question: Which statement describes the effects of adrenaline on the body?
options: It decreases heart rate so the body saves energy
It reduces the glucose supply to the muscles
It increases heart rate and boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles
It increases the reabsorption of water in the kidneys
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases heart rate and boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles
questions.explanation: This is the specification wording. It prepares the body for fight or flight. Water reabsorption is controlled by ADH.

questions.question: Which statement describes negative feedback?
options: A change from the normal level triggers a response that reverses the change
A change triggers a response that makes the change bigger
A hormone that always lowers levels in the body
A nervous reflex that does not involve the brain
markScheme: 1 mark: A change from the normal level triggers a response that reverses the change
questions.explanation: Negative feedback opposes the change in either direction. Making the change bigger would be positive feedback.

questions.question:
The concentration of thyroxine in the blood rises above the normal level.
What happens next?
options: The thyroid gland releases more thyroxine
The adrenal glands release more adrenaline
Release of TSH from the pituitary is inhibited, so less thyroxine is released
markScheme: 1 mark: Release of TSH from the pituitary is inhibited, so less thyroxine is released
questions.explanation: High thyroxine inhibits TSH release. With less TSH, the thyroid is stimulated less, so thyroxine falls back to normal.

questions.question: Which gland releases TSH, the hormone that stimulates the thyroid gland?
markScheme: 1 mark: Pituitary gland
questions.explanation: The pituitary is often called the master gland because its hormones, such as TSH, control other glands.

questions.question:
Adrenaline boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles.
Why does this help the body in a 'fight or flight' situation?
options: Muscles store glucose as fat for later
Oxygen and glucose make muscle cells divide
More respiration in muscle cells releases more energy for contraction
markScheme: 1 mark: More respiration in muscle cells releases more energy for contraction
questions.explanation: Oxygen and glucose are the reactants of aerobic respiration. More respiration means more energy for the muscles to contract quickly and strongly.

questions.question:
The concentration of thyroxine in a person's blood falls below the normal level.
Which sequence describes the body's response?
options: Less inhibition of the pituitary → more TSH released → thyroid releases more thyroxine
More inhibition of the pituitary → less TSH → less thyroxine
Thyroid releases TSH → pituitary releases more thyroxine
markScheme: 1 mark: Less inhibition of the pituitary → more TSH released → thyroid releases more thyroxine
questions.explanation: With low thyroxine, the brake on TSH release is reduced, so TSH rises and stimulates the thyroid. This raises thyroxine back to normal: negative feedback.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of negative feedback?
options: A rise in oestrogen causing a surge in LH
Uterus contractions in labour becoming stronger and stronger
Blood that is too dilute causing less ADH to be released, so more water is lost in urine
markScheme: 1 mark: Blood that is too dilute causing less ADH to be released, so more water is lost in urine
questions.explanation: Here the response (less ADH, more water lost) reverses the change (too much water). The LH surge and labour contractions amplify a change rather than reverse it, and fear causing adrenaline release is a response to a stimulus, not a feedback loop.

questions.question:
Complete the sentence.
As well as stimulating the basal metabolic rate, thyroxine is important in
markScheme: 1 mark: growth and development
questions.explanation: The specification states that thyroxine plays an important role in growth and development. This is why low thyroxine in children is screened for at birth.

questions.question:
Name the hormone produced by the thyroid gland.
Give one function of this hormone.
markScheme: 1 mark: thyroxine
1 mark: stimulates the basal metabolic rate / important in growth and development
questions.explanation: Thyroxine has two roles named in the specification: basal metabolic rate, and growth and development.

questions.question: Give two effects of adrenaline on the body.
acceptedAnswers: more oxygen and glucose to brain
markScheme: 1 mark: increases heart rate
1 mark: boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles
questions.explanation: Both effects prepare the body for fight or flight. Increased breathing rate is also accepted by many markers, but the two specification points are safest.

questions.question: Explain why adrenaline is said to prepare the body for 'fight or flight'.
acceptedAnswers: more oxygen and glucose to muscles
markScheme: 1 mark: increases heart rate so more oxygen and glucose are delivered to the muscles (and brain)
1 mark: so more respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction / ready to run away or fight
questions.explanation: Fight or flight requires rapid, strong muscle action. Adrenaline increases the supply of the reactants for respiration.

questions.explanation: Describe both directions of change to show how negative feedback returns the level to normal.

questions.question:
The pituitary gland is sometimes called the 'master gland'.
Use the control of thyroxine to explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the pituitary releases hormones (TSH) in response to body conditions
1 mark: which act on / control other glands, e.g. TSH stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes several hormones that act on other glands, so it controls them.

questions.question:
A person has an underactive thyroid gland and produces too little thyroxine.
Suggest two symptoms the person may have.
Explain one of the symptoms you have suggested.
markScheme: 1 mark: any two symptoms: tiredness / lack of energy; weight gain; feeling cold; slow growth (in children)
1 mark: explanation linked to low basal metabolic rate, e.g. less energy released by chemical reactions so less heat produced
questions.explanation: Low thyroxine means a low basal metabolic rate, so less energy is used and less heat released. In children growth and development are affected.

questions.explanation: Normally thyroxine inhibits TSH release. Without thyroxine, the feedback loop is broken and TSH rises.

questions.question:
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine.
People with too little iodine in their diet may develop a swollen thyroid gland.
Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: too little iodine means less thyroxine is made
1 mark: low thyroxine means less inhibition of the pituitary, so more TSH is released
1 mark: TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid, which grows / swells
questions.explanation: This applies the thyroxine feedback loop to an unfamiliar context, which is typical of grade 7 to 9 questions. Each step must be linked.

questions.question:
A student measured her resting heart rate three times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean resting heart rate.

headers: Heart rate in beats per minute

questions.explanation: Add the values and divide by the number of readings. Repeating measurements and taking a mean improves the reliability of the result.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a person's heart rate before and after adrenaline was released into their blood.
Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate.

headers: Heart rate in beats per minute

markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 126 − 72 = 54
questions.explanation: Divide the increase by the original value. Using 126 as the denominator gives 42.9 %, which is wrong.

questions.question:
A person's basal metabolic rate is 7200 kJ per day.
An overactive thyroid gland increases the person's basal metabolic rate by 25%.
Calculate the new basal metabolic rate.
markScheme: 1 mark: 7200 + 1800 = 9000 kJ per day
questions.explanation: Find 25 % then add it on, or multiply by 1.25. Extra thyroxine raises basal metabolic rate, so the person may lose weight and feel hot.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a person's heart rate at rest and when the person is frightened.
Each heartbeat pumps 70 cm³ of blood.
Calculate the increase in the volume of blood pumped each minute when the person is frightened.
Give your answer in dm³.

headers: Heart rate in beats per minute

markScheme: 1 mark: increase in heart rate = 112 − 64 = 48 beats per minute
questions.explanation: Alternatively, 112 × 70 = 7840 cm³ and 64 × 70 = 4480 cm³; the difference is 3360 cm³. Remember 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

questions.question: Explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline in the body.
markScheme: Indicative content: thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland; it stimulates the basal metabolic rate; it is important for growth and development; its level is controlled by negative feedback; adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands; released in times of fear or stress; increases heart rate; boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles; more respiration releasing energy for muscle contraction; prepares the body for fight or flight.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of both hormones, including source glands and effects.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic effects of one or both hormones.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Name the gland, the trigger and the effect for each hormone, and say why the effect is useful.

questions.question: Explain how the level of thyroxine in the blood is controlled by negative feedback. You may include a labelled diagram in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: thyroxine is released by the thyroid gland; thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate; the pituitary gland releases TSH; TSH travels in the blood and stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine; if thyroxine rises above normal, it inhibits TSH release from the pituitary; less TSH means the thyroid releases less thyroxine; thyroxine level falls back to normal; if thyroxine falls below normal, there is less inhibition; more TSH is released; the thyroid releases more thyroxine; level rises back to normal; negative feedback means the response reverses the change; the level fluctuates around a normal value.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): full explanation of the loop for both a rise and a fall, using stimulate and inhibit correctly and linking to the idea that the change is reversed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): description of the loop in one direction, or both directions with some errors.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. thyroid makes thyroxine, pituitary makes TSH.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Showing both directions (too high and too low) demonstrates understanding of negative feedback and is needed for Level 3.

questions.question:
Compare the hormones adrenaline and thyroxine.
In your answer you should include:
• where each hormone is made
• when each hormone is released
• the effects of each hormone and how they help the body.
markScheme: Indicative content, similarities: both are hormones released by endocrine glands into the blood; both affect energy use/respiration in cells; both act on many target organs.

Differences: adrenaline is made by the adrenal glands, thyroxine by the thyroid gland; adrenaline is released in times of fear or stress, thyroxine is released continuously with its level kept steady by negative feedback (via TSH from the pituitary); adrenaline increases heart rate and boosts oxygen and glucose delivery to brain and muscles, thyroxine stimulates basal metabolic rate and growth and development; adrenaline gives a rapid, short-term response (fight or flight), thyroxine has longer-term effects.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison with clear similarities and differences across source, trigger, effect and purpose.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some valid comparisons, or a description of each hormone without direct comparison.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic facts about one or both hormones.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: 'Compare' needs linked statements such as 'whereas' or 'but'. Two separate descriptions without comparison will not reach Level 3.
